name: Phom
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Burling, Robbins & L. Amon Phom. 1998. Phom phonology and word list. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 21(2): 13-42.
catalog_locator: p. 14 (§1.0 Introduction, last paragraph), p. 19 (§5.0 TONES, opening), p. 21 (§6.0 Assimilation across syllable boundaries, second paragraph); the scan, pp. 2, 7, 9
catalog_quote: Phom does turn out to be a tone language, and like many such languages of East and Southeast Asia, its sound system is most easily described in terms of its syllables and their parts: 1. Initial consonants, 2. Vowels, 3. Final consonants, 4. Tones. [p. 14] ... 5.0. TONES. Three distinct tones can occur with most types of syllables and they are quite transparent. Syllables ending with /ʔ/, however, show no tonal contrast. [p. 19] ... Except for this relatively modest amount of assimilation, we have found no other ways in which syllables influence their neighbors. So far as we have discovered, any type of syllable can follow any other type. There appear to be no restrictions on tone sequences, and we have had no difficulty in identifying the tones of polysyllabic words with the tones found on one-syllable words. Nor does the Phom language have the kind of “half” or “minor” syllables that characterize many of the Tibeto-Burman languages spoken further to the east, in which the initial syllables of many words have restricted phonological complexity compared with the “full” syllables that follow. [p. 21]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Phom is described as a lexical tone language: every syllable carries one of three tones (/55/ high level, /33/ mid level, /31/ mid-to-low falling; glottal-final syllables toneless), polysyllables are simply concatenations of fully toned syllables with no reduced or 'minor' syllables and no tone-sequence restrictions. No source examined describes word stress, accent, or prominence at all; none says stress is absent either. Bano 2008 (p. 168) adds a tone-placement generalization ('the high tones are usually marked on the second syllable' of bi-/tri-syllabic words, on the first if the second is glottal-stopped) and Phom 2018 (p. 112) finds tone alternation 'biased to the left sided syllables' in derived disyllables, but both concern tone, not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: syllables ending in /ʔ/ show no tonal contrast (Burling & Phom p. 19); tone /31/ is rare on stopped syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (monosyllables and compounds/derived polysyllables in citation form). Phom 2018 recorded words in isolation and in a carrier sentence and found tones stable across contexts (no tone sandhi). Burling & Phom's data come from co-author L. Amon Phom, a native speaker from the lower Tamlu area; Phom 2018 (pp. 12-16) notes dialect differences (Yongyah standard vs. lower Tamlu villages, e.g. absence of /ɣ/ there).
new_statements.identity_note: All three opened sources describe the Phom of Longleng district, Nagaland (phom1236). Burling & Phom 1998 reflects one speaker (L. Amon Phom) from the lower Tamlu villages; Phom 2018 uses speakers of the Yongyah (standard) dialect and lists dialect differences in ch. 1 (pp. 12-16) and Appendix III. No separate glottocodes exist for these dialects.

tone_statements.citation: Kumar, Braj Bihari. 1973. Phom vyākaraṇ kī rūparekhā [An outline of Phom grammar; in Hindi]. Kohima: Nagaland Bhasha Parishad.
tone_statements.quote: Stage II is best represented by Phom, where category D has fully merged with B and there is no influence on the tone system of the syllable structure beyond that. Category C is posited as a reflex of *creaky, which is likely the motivating factor in the merger, possibly due to creak being realised as a low pitch as it is in Tangsa-Nocte varieties for which it is present, and CVC syllables otherwise having a low tone. Both are 33: contours today in Phom, whereas reflexes of group A are 55: and those of B are 31: based on Burling and Phom (1998).
tone_statements.summary: Three Chao values (55, 31, 33) given for Phom after Burling & Phom 1998; no explicit count stated. Text says D merged 'with B' but values and Fig. 2 show D merging with C. Nothing on TBU or stress.

sources.locator: p. 14 (§1.0 Introduction), p. 19 (§5.0 Tones), p. 21 (§6.0 Polysyllables); pp. 2, 7, 9
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Phom is 'a tone language' (p. 14); section 5.0 TONES (p. 19) gives three tones /55/ high level, /33/ mid level, /31/ falling; syllables in /-ʔ/ show no tonal contrast; 'no restrictions on tone sequences', tones of polysyllables identified with those of monosyllables, and no reduced 'half'/'minor' syllables (p. 21). The word 'stress' does not occur in the scanned text (only 'strongly accented' in a comparison with an English vowel, p. 16).

sources.note: No stress rule. 'Stress' appears only as a Chomsky-Halle distinctive-feature category ('5.9.3 Prosodic features.. (a) Stress (b) Length', p. 165) that is never applied to Phom data, and in 'final unstressed vowel schwa' in an apocope rule (p. 185). Tones (5.10, pp. 167-170): 'In Phom language, tones are phonemic.. There are three register tones in Phom' (high, low, medial/level); 'In bi-syllabic and tri-syllabic words, the high tones are usually marked on the second syllable, but if the second syllable is followed by a glottal stop, the tone is marked on the first syllables of the words' (p.…
Consonant chart copied from Burling (1998); nothing on tone or stress; links only to the sealang copy of Burling & Phom.

sources.citation: Phom, Phongshak. 2018 [submitted 2016, awarded 2017]. An Acoustic Study of Lexical Tones in Phom. PhD thesis, Department of Phonetics and Spoken English, The English and Foreign Languages University, Hyderabad (supervisor Dominic Savio).
sources.note: No stress finding. Lists 'the effect of the stress plays on the tone in the language' among its objectives (p. 104) but reports none; one offhand remark that consonant clusters in derived polysyllables 'are pronounced with the same amount of stress as different syllables' (p. 29-30). Acoustically confirms three tones (high and mid level, low falling; p. 111); in disyllables both syllables keep their lexical tones, but tone alternation is 'biased' to one syllable: 'In derived disyllables, the tone change is biased to the left sided syllables, while the right sided syllables or suffixes usually…
